newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's CPMF tax seen raising cost of bank loans.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's CPMF tax seen raising cost of bank loans.

text.p: A new Brazilian tax which will levy a 0.2 percent charge on financial transactions is unlikely to pressure inflation, but is expected to raise interest rates on bank loans and encourage long-term investments, analysts said.
"The most significant impact of the tax will be seen on credit costs and the allocation of financial investments," said Odair Abate, chief economist at Lloyds Bank Brazil unit.
"The effects of the CPMF tax on inflation will be minimal," he added.
Analysts said the so-called CPMF tax is likely to make bank loans more expensive for borrowers as banks will tend to raise the interest rates they charge to compensate for the cost of the tax.
They also predict a change in the investment funds industry, with investors withdrawing money from local short-term funds as the 0.2 percent tax could eliminate all or most of their gains.
Currently, short-term funds, whose assets total some 22 billion reais, have been offering monthly yields of 0.39 percent.

Created to provide some 400 million reais a month for Brazil's health services, the CPMF tax will take effect Thursday for one year. The levy has been criticized by analysts and some government officials who complain it is an inefficient way to raise revenue.
It was passed by Congress last year following heavy lobbying by former Health Minister Adib Jatene, who resigned shortly afterwards.

In addition to raising rates on bank loans, analysts said the CPMF tax could reduce the availability of credit if most of the money in the short-term funds moves to checking accounts, which are subject to higher bank reserve requirements.
Banks must hold 75 percent of deposits in their checking accounts in reserve.

Central Bank chief Gustavo Loyola told Gazeta Mercantil newspaper today that the Central Bank would monitor the effects of the CPMF tax, which could lead to an alteration in the current bank reserve requirements.
"We can increase some requirements and lower others where it's needed. But it's still too early to say," Loyola was quoted as saying.
Regarding the impact of the CPMF tax on foreign investment in Brazilian equities, analysts said the tax is unlikely to scare foreigners away from the local exchanges.
"Considering the bolsa's high investment return, the 0.2 percent will make no difference," an analyst said.
Foreigners will pay the 0.2 percent CPMF tax on starting and ending their stock investment. Transactions involving foreign capital within the bolsas will be exempt.
